projects.name: Wheeled SPOT Trajectory DEMO | NVIDIA Isaac Sim & Isaac Lab
projects.description:
In this video I demonstrate a wheeled Spot-style robot inspired by Boston Dynamics Spot that I trained using NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab to autonomously complete a route defined by five waypoints.

The robot uses reinforcement learning for low-level motion and stability, combined with a high-level navigation controller that sends target XY positions to the policy. By sequentially reaching each waypoint, the robot is able to follow a full path through the environment, demonstrating reliable goal-directed navigation.

This setup shows how learned locomotion policies can be combined with waypoint-based high-level control to produce structured, repeatable robot behavior suitable for real-world navigation tasks.

All training and evaluation were performed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab, using physics-based simulation and reinforcement learning to achieve stable and precise movement.

projects.name: Vulcan-Inspired Auto-Targeting System
projects.description:
This video presents a small but powerful proof of concept demonstrating real-time visual target tracking using a PixyCam and a pair of pan-tilt servos for azimuth and elevation control.

The camera is configured to lock onto objects based on color. Once a target is detected, its position in the image is continuously translated into servo commands that keep the target centered in the camera’s field of view. In this demonstration, the system tracks an orange, a yellow apple, and a clementine, with the active target switching dynamically based on the selected color.

The same tracking commands are also sent to a second pair of servos, which mirror the camera’s motion and drive a 3D-printed Vulcan-style turret (used here purely for illustration). As the camera follows the target, the turret moves accordingly, visually showing how vision-based tracking can be mechanically coupled to a physical platform.

This project demonstrates how much can be achieved with very low-cost hardware using simple computer vision and control logic.

In a real operational system, additional calibration would be required — including accounting for the known offset between the camera and the actuator, as well as the distance to the target — in order to compute accurate aiming and alignment. However, this proof of concept clearly demonstrates the core idea: visual detection → tracking → physical actuation.

The ability to switch between different colors of interest also highlights a more general principle: the system can be extended beyond color to track targets based on arbitrary user-defined criteria, allowing a human or higher-level AI to dynamically classify objects as “interesting” or “uninteresting” and switch focus between them in real time.

This makes the project a compelling demonstration of low-cost, real-time visual servoing and target selection.

projects.name: EG-209 | Bipedal Walker
projects.description:
I took a biped robot from a raw URDF/USD-style asset to a working reinforcement learning locomotion simulation in NVIDIA Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab.

The pipeline included building usable collisions and articulation, defining an 8-DOF biped RL environment, training PPO across hundreds of parallel environments, and shaping rewards for stable, cyclic, left-right coordinated walking.

The policy has currently converged to a stable backward walk.

So yes, it walks. It just walks with a bit of moonwalk energy.

Still, that’s a real milestone: raw robot geometry → physics simulation → full episode completion → repeatable learned locomotion.

Next step: fix directionality and keep improving the gait toward forward, balanced, symmetric humanoid walking.

projects.name: Wheeled SPOT follows ball DEMO | Nvidia Isaac Sim & Isaac Lab
projects.description:
In this video I demonstrate how I trained a Spot-style quadruped robot using NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab with a curriculum-based reinforcement learning pipeline.

The robot was trained progressively, starting from basic stability and balance, then learning to drive forward and backward, rotate in place, and finally respond to high-level navigation commands.
On top of the low-level locomotion policy, I added a high-level controller that commands the robot to move to target XY positions and chase a moving ball in real time.

This layered control approach allows the robot to combine learned locomotion with goal-directed navigation, enabling complex autonomous behaviors such as waypoint tracking and dynamic target pursuit.

The project is inspired by NVIDIA’s Isaac Lab examples and workflows, adapted and extended for a Spot-like robot.

projects.name: Standing Still → Driving Forward | NVIDIA Isaac Sim & Isaac Lab
projects.description:
In this video I showcase a wheeled Spot robot (Boston Dynamics Spot ) that I trained using NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab with reinforcement learning.

The robot was trained through a curriculum to learn multiple low-level behaviors, including:

Standing stably in place

Driving forward on its wheels

Each of these behaviors was learned as a separate policy. On top of that, I implemented a high-level controller that dynamically switches between these learned policies in real time. This allows the robot to transition smoothly between standing and driving forward based on the task it needs to perform.

This demonstrates a key capability of modern robot learning systems: composing multiple learned skills into a single high-level controller, enabling more complex and flexible autonomous behavior than any single policy could achieve alone.

All training and evaluation were performed inside NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab, using physics-based simulation and reinforcement learning to produce stable, transferable robot behaviors.

projects.name: CoppeliaSim: Two-link planar manipulator, Inverse Kinematics
projects.description:
In this video, I present the results of my work after following the fantastic tutorial by Pranav Bhounsule on controlling a 2-link manipulator using forward kinematics. A huge thank you to Pranav for his clear and insightful guidance in his tutorials, which have been incredibly helpful for exploring robotics and kinematic control concepts.

This video showcases the implementation of the techniques demonstrated in the tutorial, including trajectory planning, Jacobian-based control, and smooth actuation of a robotic manipulator.

If you're interested in robotics or looking to learn about forward kinematics and control systems, I highly recommend checking out Pranav Bhounsule's original tutorial here:    • CoppeliaSim: Two-link planar manipulator, ...  .

Key Features in This Video:

Forward kinematics implementation for a 2-link manipulator.
Real-time trajectory tracking and end-effector motion.
Insights from hands-on application of tutorial concepts.
Thank you for watching! If you enjoyed this video or found it helpful, consider liking, sharing, and subscribing for more robotics-related content.

projects.name: Unitree G1 | 4 Minutes to Stability: Reinforcement Learning Converges in Isaac Sim
projects.description:
Training Unitree G1 in NVIDIA Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab to track a flat velocity command.

Initially, none of the 4096 environments reach the end of the episode.
Four minutes later, almost all of them do — showing fast RL convergence to stable standing and velocity tracking.

Honestly, I’m really impressed by how fast this converges and by what’s possible today with modern simulation and RL tools.

Hardware: Lenovo Legion 7, RTX 5070 Ti

projects.name: ROS2 on Windows using WSL2 | Real-Time Talker Listener Demo (Proof of Concept)
projects.description:
Abstract:
Created a cross-platform robotics communication stack:
Windows Host
   ├── WSL2 (Ubuntu Linux)
   │       └── ROS 2 (Humble)
   └── (future) Isaac Sim


In this video, I demonstrate a successful proof of concept of running ROS 2 (Humble) on a Windows machine using WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux).

I installed Ubuntu 22.04 inside WSL2 and set up a full ROS 2 environment. To validate the system, I ran a classic talker/listener demo, where one node publishes data and another node subscribes to it in real time.

This confirms that:

ROS 2 runs correctly inside WSL2
DDS-based communication is fully functional
Real-time publish/subscribe messaging works across nodes

This setup effectively turns a Windows machine into a Linux-based robotics development platform, enabling seamless integration with tools like NVIDIA Isaac Sim.

This is a foundational step toward building more advanced robotics systems, including:

Simulation-to-ROS integration
Robot control pipelines
AI and reinforcement learning workflows

Next step: connecting ROS 2 to Isaac Sim and controlling a robot in simulation.

items.title: Planetary Gear for 1280KV Brushless Motor
items.description: A single-stage planetary gearbox designed around a 1280KV brushless motor with a 5 mm shaft. The transmission uses one 16-tooth sun gear, three 24-tooth planet gears, and one 64-tooth internal ring gear with module 1.25 and 20° pressure angle. The planets are mounted on a carrier at 120° spacing and rotate inside the internal ring gear. The gearbox provides an approximate 5:1 reduction ratio, increasing the output torque by about 500% while reducing the output speed by 80%. The system is optimized for compact size, smooth motion, and about 0.5 Nm output torque.

items.title: Belt Actuator for Nema 17 with
items.description:
This belt-driven actuator design uses a standard NEMA 17 stepper motor (typically around 2.2 Nm torque) combined with a high-ratio belt reduction system to achieve an estimated output torque of nearly 30 Nm. The transmission provides roughly a 13–14:1 reduction ratio, significantly increasing torque while maintaining smooth, compact, and efficient operation.

The actuator was 3D printed and assembled based on the original belt-drive design by the How To Mechatronics YouTube channel, featured in the video “Cycloidal vs Belt vs Planetary - The Best 3D Printed Drive for Your Next Robotic Project?”.

items.title: The Sphere
items.description:
In collaboration with a friend who shares the same passion for engineering, we turned a concept sketched on paper into reality: a remotely controlled differential-drive spherical robot. What started as an idea evolved into a fully functional prototype through design, fabrication, electronics integration, and programming.

Our next step is to equip the robot with an onboard camera and develop autonomous decision-making capabilities, enabling it to perceive its environment and operate independently without direct human control.
